lead: A radio signal reaches the receiver along many paths, each with its own delay, strength and Doppler shift, so the received signal fades and smears. OFDM answers the smearing by splitting one fast data stream into many slow ones on closely spaced, orthogonal subcarriers, built with an inverse FFT and separated with an FFT. A cyclic prefix soaks up the echoes, and each narrow subcarrier then sees a simple flat gain. Wi-Fi, 4G LTE, 5G NR and digital TV all use it.
prereq: You need: QAM, the discrete Fourier transform and intersymbol interference (see baseband data transmission and detection).

blocks.text: The delay spread is how long the echoes keep arriving: τmax from first to last, or the rms value στ. Its frequency-domain twin is the coherence bandwidth Bc, the range over which the channel gain stays nearly the same; a common rule is Bc ≈ 1/(5στ). If the signal bandwidth is well below Bc the fading is flat (all frequencies rise and fall together); if it is wider, the fading is frequency-selective and the echoes cause intersymbol interference.

Motion adds the time dimension. The maximum Doppler shift is fd = vfc/c (v the speed, c = 3 × 108 m/s), and the coherence time, over which the channel stays nearly constant, is roughly Tc ≈ 0.423/fd. Symbols much shorter than Tc see slow fading; symbols comparable to it see fast fading.
γ̄ is the mean E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>. With no direct path the amplitude is Rayleigh distributed and the error rate falls only as 1/γ̄, against an exponential fall in AWGN.

Diversity sends or receives the same bit over independently fading paths: different times (coding with interleaving), frequencies, or antennas. Maximal-ratio combining (MRC) weights each branch by its own gain and adds them. With two branches BPSK gives Pb ≈ 3/(16γ̄²), falling as 1/γ̄²: deep fades must now happen on both branches at once.

Send N QAM symbols X[0] … X[N − 1] at the same time, each on its own subcarrier. Each lasts the useful time T<sub>u</sub>, N times longer than one serial symbol, so the same echoes are a small fraction of it.

blocks.where: Δf is the subcarrier spacing in Hz. At this spacing every subcarrier makes a whole number of cycles in T<sub>u</sub>, so they are orthogonal: the spectra overlap, but at each subcarrier's centre all the others pass through zero.

items: Map the bits to QAM symbols X[k], k = 0, 1, …, N − 1.
Take an N-point IFFT: x[n] = (1/N)Σ X[k]e<sup>j2πkn/N</sup>, n = 0, …, N − 1.
Copy the last G samples to the front as the cyclic prefix and send N + G samples.
At the receiver drop the first G samples and take an N-point FFT to get Y[k].
Divide Y[k] by the channel gain H[k] and slice each subcarrier's QAM point.

blocks.where: H[k] is the channel's frequency response at subcarrier k and W[k] the noise. Equalisation is one complex division per subcarrier instead of a long time-domain filter. The FFT needs about N log<sub>2</sub> N operations instead of N².

sections.h3: The cyclic prefix and practical limits

blocks.text: The physical channel convolves the signal with its impulse response. Because the prefix repeats the end of the block, the useful block the receiver keeps equals a circular convolution of x[n] with the channel, provided the prefix is at least as long as the channel's delay spread. The FFT turns a circular convolution into the product H[k]X[k], and the previous symbol's echoes die inside the prefix: no ISI, no inter-carrier interference (ICI).
T is the full symbol time; T<sub>cp</sub> = G/B with B = NΔf the sample rate. A prefix shorter than τ<sub>max</sub> lets ISI and ICI in.

items: Overhead: the prefix carries no new data, so rates use T, not Tu; Tcp/T is lost.
Peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR): many subcarriers can add in phase, so the amplifier must back off.
Synchronisation: a carrier frequency offset of a fraction of Δf breaks orthogonality and causes ICI.

Fading per subcarrier: OFDM removes ISI, not fading; a subcarrier in a deep notch is lost, so OFDM systems add coding across subcarriers (frequency diversity). OFDMA shares subcarriers among users, as in the LTE downlink.

examples.question: An OFDM system uses N = 64 subcarriers in 20 MHz, a 16-sample cyclic prefix and 64-QAM on every subcarrier. Find Δf, T<sub>u</sub>, T<sub>cp</sub>, T, the prefix overhead and the uncoded bit rate. Repeat the rate for 48 data subcarriers and rate-¾ coding, as in Wi-Fi.
steps: Sample time 1/(20 MHz) = 50 ns, so T<sub>cp</sub> = 16 × 50 ns = 0.8 µs and T = 4.0 µs.
64-QAM gives 6 bits per subcarrier: 64 × 6 = 384 bits per symbol, so R = 384/4.0 µs = 96 Mb/s.
With 48 data subcarriers: 48 × 6 = 288 bits per symbol → 72 Mb/s; with rate-¾ coding 288 × 0.75/4.0 µs = 54 Mb/s.
examples.answer: Δf = 312.5 kHz, T<sub>u</sub> = 3.2 µs, T<sub>cp</sub> = 0.8 µs, T = 4.0 µs, 20% overhead; 96 Mb/s uncoded on all 64, 54 Mb/s with 48 data subcarriers and rate-¾ coding.

examples.question: The system above runs at f<sub>c</sub> = 2 GHz in a car at 108 km/h on a channel with σ<sub>τ</sub> = 0.2 µs. Is the fading slow or fast, flat or frequency-selective for the whole signal and for one subcarrier? Find P<sub>b</sub> for BPSK at a mean E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> of 20 dB in Rayleigh fading, without and with two-branch MRC.
steps: T = 4 µs is about 530 times shorter than T<sub>c</sub>: slow fading, H[k] stays put over hundreds of symbols.
B<sub>c</sub> ≈ 1/(5 × 0.2 µs) = 1 MHz. The 20 MHz signal is frequency-selective; a 312.5 kHz subcarrier is narrower than B<sub>c</sub>, so it sees nearly flat fading.
γ̄ = 100: P<sub>b</sub> = ½[1 − √(100/101)] = 2.48 × 10<sup>−3</sup> (≈ 1/400). In AWGN at 20 dB it would be about 10<sup>−45.</sup>
Two-branch MRC: P<sub>b</sub> = 1.84 × 10<sup>−5</sup> (≈ 3/(16 × 100²) = 1.88 × 10<sup>−5</sup>), about 135 times better.
examples.answer: Slow fading; frequency-selective over 20 MHz but flat per subcarrier; P<sub>b</sub> = 2.48 × 10<sup>−3</sup> without diversity and 1.84 × 10<sup>−5</sup> with two-branch MRC.

traps: Bit rates use T = T<sub>u</sub> + T<sub>cp</sub>, not T<sub>u</sub>; the prefix is overhead.
OFDM removes ISI when T<sub>cp</sub> ≥ τ<sub>max</sub>; it does not remove fading. Each subcarrier still has its own gain H[k].
f<sub>d</sub> = vf<sub>c</sub>/c is the maximum Doppler shift; T<sub>c</sub> ≈ 0.423/f<sub>d</sub> is a rule of thumb, and some books use 1/f<sub>d</sub>. State the rule you use.
A prefix exactly equal to the delay spread is enough; one even slightly shorter lets the previous symbol leak in.
Bits per OFDM symbol = (number of data subcarriers) × log<sub>2</sub> M; forgetting either factor is common.

quiz.q: What does the IFFT do in an OFDM transmitter?
quiz.a: It turns N QAM symbols, one per subcarrier, into N time samples of one OFDM symbol.

quiz.q: Why can OFDM subcarriers overlap without interfering?
quiz.a: At spacing 1/T<sub>u</sub> each makes a whole number of cycles in T<sub>u</sub>, so they are orthogonal; at each subcarrier's centre the others' spectra are zero.

quiz.q: Δf = 15 kHz and the prefix is 10% of T<sub>u</sub>. Find T<sub>u</sub>, T<sub>cp</sub> and T.
quiz.a: T<sub>u</sub> = 66.67 µs, T<sub>cp</sub> = 6.67 µs, T = 73.33 µs.

quiz.q: The 20 MHz, 64-subcarrier, 16-sample-prefix system uses QPSK on all subcarriers. Find the uncoded rate.
Find f<sub>d</sub> and T<sub>c</sub> at 2.4 GHz and 36 km/h.
quiz.a: v = 10 m/s; f<sub>d</sub> = 80 Hz; T<sub>c</sub> ≈ 0.423/80 = 5.3 ms.

quiz.q: Why does diversity help so much in Rayleigh fading?
quiz.a: Errors come mainly from deep fades. With two independent branches both must fade at once, so P<sub>b</sub> falls as 1/γ̄² instead of 1/γ̄.

quiz.q: What goes wrong if T<sub>cp</sub> < τ<sub>max</sub>?
quiz.a: The previous symbol's echoes reach into the FFT window (ISI) and the block is no longer a circular convolution, so the subcarriers leak into each other (ICI).

beyond: Not for the exam. 5G NR scales the subcarrier spacing (15, 30, 60, 120 kHz) to the band and uses DFT-spread OFDM on the uplink to cut the PAPR; MIMO-OFDM adds space diversity and multiplexing per subcarrier. OTFS is studied for high-speed trains and aircraft, where Doppler is large. Search next: MIMO-OFDM, channel estimation with pilots, OTFS.

Bottom: one 4.0 µs OFDM symbol, a 0.8 µs cyclic prefix before the 3.2 µs useful part; an echo of the previous symbol delayed less than 0.8 µs dies inside the prefix.

spec.aria: Top: overlapping sinc-shaped spectra centred every 312.5 kilohertz, with a marker showing the neighbours pass through zero at the centre of one subcarrier. Bottom: a time line with the previous symbol, a 0.8 microsecond cyclic prefix and a 3.2 microsecond useful part, and a delayed echo of the previous symbol ending inside the prefix.
